docs.title: Home
docs.text:
Your AI teammate for site reliability

Azure SRE Agent NanoHack

Observe → Detect → Investigate → Decide → Remediate → Verify → Learn

New to the agent? Skim the optional primer Meet the SRE Agent first and learn about permissions, run modes, skills and subagents in a couple of minutes.

What you need before you start

Your facilitator has already provisioned your Aetherion environment in your own resource group. You need PowerShell 7, Azure CLI, kubectl, Git and the GitHub CLI, plus a GitHub personal access token for Challenge 6. Set up your environment walks through all of it.

docs.title: Keep Aetherion AirOps flying
docs.text:
You are the new reliability team for a global airline platform. In one focused session you will pair with the Azure SRE Agent: first guiding it hands-on, then trusting it to recover a live microservices estate on its own within guardrails, moving from human-approved fixes to bounded autonomy before peak departure.

Self-paced · 4 acts · 6 challenges · ~3–4 hours

Start here

docs.title: The journey
docs.text:
• Act I · Foundation Orient

    Onboard the SRE Agent in read-only mode and capture a healthy baseline.

  • Act II · Human-Guided Operations Respond

    Detect and investigate an incident read-only, then recover under human approval.

  • Act III · Autonomous Automate

    Let the agent remediate autonomously within bounds and arm a Sev1 response plan.

  • Act IV · Major Incident Command

    Restore global check-in during a multi-service incident, then brief airline leadership.

Finished early? Two optional extras are in the Optional extras tab: ground the agent in Aetherion's runbooks, and build a specialist subagent and skill.

docs.title: Challenge 1 · Onboard the Agent and Establish the Baseline
docs.text:
Challenge 01 of 06 · Act I: Foundation

Time: ~45 min · Run mode: Review · Access: your resource group only

Situation. You are Sam Rivera, on your first shift as a reliability engineer at Aetherion AirOps. Every tile is green. Beside you is Aria, the Azure SRE Agent: a new teammate with no access to anything yet.

Mission. Create the agent on the Azure OpenAI model provider, scope it to your resource group in Review mode, capture a healthy baseline, and schedule a daily health check.

New here? Meet Aetherion takes two minutes.

Start this challenge

./scripts/start-challenge.ps1 1

No fault is injected. If the Operations Center is not all green, run ./scripts/reset-environment.ps1 and wait a few minutes before you capture a baseline.

Model provider: select Azure OpenAI (GPT / ChatGPT). Never Anthropic.

Regulatory requirement. The create wizard labels Azure OpenAI as Covered by EU Data Boundary commitments. Anthropic is labelled Excluded from EU Data Boundary (data may be processed in the United States) even though the wizard badges it Preferred. Azure OpenAI is preselected: leave it. Check the label before you click Next. You can see and change the provider later in the agent's settings, so confirm it there too.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Check the board. Read the Operations Center while it is green. That is your reference for the day.
  2. Confirm telemetry. Open Grafana and check that AKS and Application Insights are reporting.
  3. Create the agent. In your resource group, on Azure OpenAI, in Review mode. Give it read access to your code, logs and resource group.
  4. Capture the baseline. Ask the agent for a baseline of the aetherion namespace, then spot-check its numbers.
  5. Schedule it. Have the agent re-run that check every morning so drift shows up early.

docs.title: Suggested prompt
docs.text:
Paste into the agent chat

Generate an operational baseline for the aetherion namespace: running services and ready replicas; dependencies (PostgreSQL, Redis, what sits behind the API); normal latency for booking (check-in) and the flight board; and the top signals to watch. Support every finding with telemetry and make no changes.

docs.title: Success criteria
docs.text:
• All tiles are healthy and Grafana shows live metrics.
  • The agent uses the Azure OpenAI provider, is scoped to your resource group only, and runs in Review mode.
  • You hold a baseline captured while healthy, and its replica counts and latency match the Ops Center and Grafana.
  • A scheduled daily health check exists.

Verify your work

./scripts/check-challenge.ps1 1

Two of the checks are yes/no questions about the connection and your baseline. Answer honestly.

Hints
  • Create the agent in the same resource group as the platform and keep it in Review mode.
  • Ask one specific question about namespace health rather than browsing pod by pod.
  • Trust measured latency; verify configuration values (CPU limits, replica counts) yourself.
Stuck? Step by step Task 3 · Create the agent
  1. Portal → Azure SRE Agent → Create. Subscription: the one your facilitator gave you. Resource group: your group (rg-aetherion-nano-…). Region: Sweden Central.
  2. Agent name: aetherion-sre-agent. It must not share its first 15 characters with your resource group name.
  3. Application Insights: Create new (the agent's own, separate from the app's).
  4. Model provider: choose Azure OpenAI and confirm it says Covered by EU Data Boundary commitments.
  5. Review + create → Create, then Full setup and connect:
    • Code → GitHub → Your account → add your copy of aetherion-airops-platform. Code Access only reads the repo, so do not spend your PAT here (it is for Challenge 6).
    • Logs → Log Analytics Workspace → the app's aetherion-law (not the agent's own workspace…).
    • Azure resources → Resource group → only your group, at Reader. Never Subscription; leave out the MC_… group.
  6. Leave Incidents and Knowledge for later; Challenge 4 connects Incidents.

Your copy, never the lab repo

The lab repo holds the answers and fault scripts. The agent must only see <your-account>/aetherion-airops-platform.

Check it took. Ask "List the resources in my resource group", then "Restart a deployment": in Review mode it must ask for approval, not act. Ask "Which log sources and repositories are you connected to?" It should name aetherion-law and your repo. If Builder → Code Access shows your repo as Ready and Builder → Connectors lists Log Analytics, you are set.

The "won't change anything" guarantee comes from Review mode, not from the role being read-only.

Task 4 · Capture the baseline

Paste the prompt above with the board green. Spot-check 2 to 3 numbers (replicas, booking latency) against the tiles and Grafana. To check a configuration value:

kubectl get deploy gateway -n aetherion -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].resources}'
Task 5 · Schedule it

In the same chat thread as Task 4, ask:

Schedule this baseline to run every morning at 08:00 UTC and alert me on drift from normal.

Include the time zone or the agent will stop and ask. You can also use Scheduled tasks in the portal.

docs.title: Challenge 2 · Detect and Investigate Without Touching Production
docs.text:
Challenge 02 of 06 · Act II: Human-Guided Operations

Time: ~40 min · Run mode: Review · Access: read-only investigation

Situation. Online check-in has slowed to a crawl. Requests that took milliseconds now take seconds, and the booking / check-in tile has gone amber just as traffic climbs toward a departure peak. Is check-in buckling under the surge, or did something change?

Mission. Confirm the slowdown from live signals and form a hypothesis for the likely cause, backed by at least two independent signals, without changing anything. Challenge 3 fixes it.

Start this challenge

./scripts/start-challenge.ps1 2

Give it two or three minutes. Latency climbs from milliseconds to seconds and stays there, while every request still succeeds, which is itself a clue.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Confirm the symptom. Compare check-in latency now with your Challenge 1 baseline, using the Operations Center and Grafana.
  2. Correlate read-only. Have the agent line up booking request duration against CPU, replicas, dependency calls and load.
  3. Record your hypothesis. Capture the likely cause, the two signals behind it, and the recovery you would propose. Do not perform it.

docs.title: Suggested prompt
docs.text:
Paste into the agent chat

Check-in has slowed to a crawl. Investigate read-only and tell me the most likely cause, with the evidence behind it. Change nothing.

That is deliberately thin, as it would be at 18:12. The first answer will be broad. Push back, and notice which follow-up moves it forward: that is the skill this challenge teaches.

docs.title: Success criteria
docs.text:
• You have confirmed the slowdown and can name the affected service and user-facing path.
  • You can name the most likely cause, backed by two independent signals, and separate the surge from the change that caused it.
  • You made no change to production.

Verify your work

./scripts/check-challenge.ps1 2
Hints
  • Start from the delta against your baseline, over the same time window.
  • A starved service is busy. This one is not: CPU is low, nothing restarted, every request succeeds. It is waiting on something. What does booking call besides its database?
  • Compare the live workload with what the repository's manifest declares. The gap is the finding.
  • Still stuck? Ask: "Analyze the check-in path read-only. Correlate booking duration with CPU, replicas, dependency call durations and load over the last 30 minutes, check recent rollouts, and compare the live workload with the repository manifest. Give the most likely cause with evidence. Change nothing."
Stuck? Step by step Task 1 · Confirm the symptom

Open the Operations Center and note the booking tile's p95 and error rate, then the Grafana dashboard for the same window. Compare with your baseline: milliseconds became seconds, yet nothing fails. A flat, elevated latency is rarely load.

Task 2 · Correlate read-only

Paste the prompt above. Look for signals that disagree: latency up while CPU, replicas and errors are normal. Something is being waited on, not overloaded. Then ask the agent to compare the running workload with the manifest in your connected repo. Stay read-only.

Task 3 · Record your hypothesis

Summarise this investigation in under 200 words: the likely root cause, the two independent signals, and the least-disruptive recovery you would propose. Do not remediate.

Keep this chat thread open for Challenge 3, or save it with "save this to your knowledge".

Write down one number

Note how many minutes passed between start-challenge.ps1 2 and a defensible hypothesis. You will compare it with the agent's speed in Challenge 5.

Proceed to Challenge 3 · Controlled Recovery →

docs.title: Challenge 3 · Controlled Recovery
docs.text:
Challenge 03 of 06 · Act II: Human-Guided Operations

Time: ~25 min · Run mode: Review, approved writes · Access: every action approved by you

Situation. Your check-in hypothesis is solid. Elena Vasquez, Aetherion's operations director, wants it fixed safely, with a human in the loop. The incident from Challenge 2 is still open.

Mission. Recover check-in with the least-disruptive action, under your approval, and verify it from telemetry.

Start this challenge

./scripts/start-challenge.ps1 3

This continues the Challenge 2 incident. No new fault is added.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Plan the fix. Ask the agent to turn your hypothesis into a concrete booking remediation plan and to name the permission it needs.
  2. Recover under approval. Keep the agent in Review, approve the least-disruptive fix, and confirm latency is back to baseline.

docs.title: Suggested prompt
docs.text:
Paste into the agent chat

Check-in is still slow. Propose a fix. Don't change anything yet.

Whatever it proposes, make it name the permission each action needs before it goes near production.

docs.title: Success criteria
docs.text:
• Check-in is fixed by a least-disruptive action you approved in Review mode, not by ungoverned automation.
  • booking is healthy, latency is back to baseline, and the setting the change altered matches what the repository declares. Compensating around it is not a fix.

Verify your work

./scripts/check-challenge.ps1 3
Hints
  • Ask for a plan before any action. The plan names the permission the write needs, and it is what you approve.
  • The safe fix puts back exactly what the last change took away. It should not restart the cache, touch the database or go near the nodes.
  • Still stuck? Ask: "Turn my check-in hypothesis into a remediation plan for booking. Restore it to exactly what the repository manifest declares, not a value you choose, and tell me what permission the action needs."
Stuck? Step by step Task 1 · Plan the fix

Paste the prompt above. The agent should say exactly what it will change and which permission that needs.

A plan is not a pending action

No Approve button appears yet. That is correct: in Review mode the card only appears when the agent attempts a write. When you are happy with the plan, say "Apply the booking remediation now."

Task 2 · Recover under approval

Read the exact command on the approval card, then select Approve action. One instruction queues one action. Then confirm booking latency is back to baseline and that no override is left on the deployment.

  • What gated the write? Your run mode, not the agent's Azure role. Permissions decide what the agent can reach; run mode decides whether it asks first.
  • Who made the change? The card says "Agent permissions will be used": the write runs as the agent's managed identity, so the Activity Log names the agent, not you. Remember this in Challenge 6.
  • Check the change record. kubectl rollout history deploy/booking -n aetherion shows the bad change and the fix with the same change cause, because the fix did not record why. That is why teams insist on pipelines that leave a record.

Up next: let the agent act on its own

Every write so far waited for your approval. Next, a minor incident is safe enough to hand to the agent.

Proceed to Challenge 4 · Autonomous Recovery →

docs.title: Challenge 4 · Autonomous Recovery and Sev1 Plan
docs.text:
Challenge 04 of 06 · Act III: Autonomous

Time: ~30 min (+15 optional cost tasks) · Run mode: Autonomous, bounded · Access: no per-action approval

Situation. Every write so far waited for your approval. Now a minor issue appears: the baggage service returns errors to a slice of traffic. Bags still move, no flight is grounded, and the fix is one you have already seen. That is exactly when it is safe to let the agent act autonomously while you supervise.

Mission. Let the agent recover baggage on its own within guardrails, then arm a Sev1 response plan for your own alert, so the next major incident triggers your agent before you reach Challenge 5.

Start this challenge

./scripts/start-challenge.ps1 4

Give it a couple of minutes. The errors show once enough traffic has hit the affected slice. The script prints your alert name. Keep it: you need it in Task 4.

Your alert name is unique to you. Your plan must filter on it.

Everyone in this subscription has a look-alike Sev1 alert, and each agent scans every alert in the subscription. A plan filtered only on Sev1 reacts to other attendees' alerts, and theirs react to yours, so an agent can take (and acknowledge) someone else's incident. Your plan must set Title contains to your exact alert name. Find it with:

(Get-Content ./scripts/.env.aetherion.json | ConvertFrom-Json).incidentAlertName

It looks like aetherion-major-incident-a1b2c3. It is also in the portal under Monitor → Alerts → Alert rules, in your resource group.

Your Sev1 alert may fire during this challenge

The baggage errors count as failed requests, so your alert can fire here too. If your agent opens a [Sev1] thread for it after you arm the plan, that is expected. Challenge 5 waits for it to clear before it starts.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Confirm the symptom. Verify the baggage errors in the Ops Center and telemetry, so you know what "recovered" looks like.
  2. Decide the bounds, then hand over. Judge whether this incident is safe to automate, switch to Autonomous, let the agent fix it end to end, then review its action log.
  3. Connect Azure Monitor. In Incidents, connect Azure Monitor as the incident platform (the default is PagerDuty, so switch it). Delete any default plan it creates.
  4. Arm the Sev1 plan on your alert. Severity Sev1, Title contains = your alert name, Autonomous, subagent left on Meta Agent, cooldown off. Challenge 5 does not work without this.

docs.title: Suggested prompt
docs.text:
Paste into the agent chat

The baggage service is returning intermittent errors to a slice of traffic while other requests succeed. Detect the fault, decide the sanctioned reversible fix, apply it autonomously, and report exactly what you changed and why it was safe to automate.

docs.title: Success criteria
docs.text:
• The agent fixed baggage autonomously, the service is healthy, and you can say why it was safe to automate: small blast radius, a reversible remedy, degraded rather than down, and a run mode you chose deliberately.
  • One enabled Sev1 plan exists, with Title contains set to your alert name, Autonomous, subagent left on Meta Agent, and cooldown disabled. It is the only plan.

Verify your work

./scripts/check-challenge.ps1 4

It grades the end state, then walks your plan setting by setting. A plan that looks right but never fires is the one failure you would not see until Challenge 5 is open.

Hints
  • What makes this safe to automate is the shape of the incident, not a permission setting. Decide that before you switch mode, then resist helping.
  • Set the plan severity to Sev1 exactly, and Title contains to your full alert name. Anything broader catches other people's alerts; anything narrower misses yours.
  • Leave Response subagent on Meta Agent so the main agent commands the whole board in Challenge 5.
Stuck? Step by step Task 1 · Confirm the symptom

Check the baggage tile and Application Insights failed requests. Some requests succeed and some fail: ask the agent what is different about the failing ones. The answer is behind the Service, not in it. kubectl get pods -n aetherion -l app=baggage --show-labels shows the same.

Task 2 · Decide the bounds, then hand over

Write down what the agent may change, what it must never touch, and how you would undo it. Set the run mode to Autonomous, let it detect, decide and fix, then review the action log.

\"Never delete\" means data, not a bad revision

The guardrails forbid deleting data resources (databases, caches, storage). Removing a workload revision that should not be serving is an ordinary, reversible rollback and the sanctioned fix.

Task 3 · Connect Azure Monitor
  1. Incidents → Connect platform → choose Azure Monitor (PagerDuty is preselected) → Save.
  2. Open Triggers & response plans. If a default quickstart plan exists, delete it: left in place it runs alongside yours and can route an incident to the wrong place or process it twice.

If an orange banner says the identity lacks Monitoring Contributor at subscription scope

Azure Monitor still connects, but the portal can only grant the role on your resource group, and the agent needs it on the subscription to scan alerts. Do not click Assign Monitoring Contributor role: you only own your resource group. Tell your proctor, who runs a script that grants it. Alerts are not processed until they have.

Task 4 · Arm the Sev1 plan on your alert

Create a response plan:

Field Value Plan name aetherion-major-incident-sev1 Severity Sev1 Title contains your exact alert name (for example aetherion-major-incident-a1b2c3) Title does not contain leave empty Response subagent leave on Meta Agent (the default) Agent autonomy level Autonomous Alert reinvestigation cooldown disable (it defaults to 3 hours and would silently block a re-run)

Then Next (it previews the incidents your filter matches) and Create. The thread title will read [Sev1] <your alert name>.

Optional · Where do the AAUs go?

Open Settings → Agent Consumption, note the two largest consumers with real figures, then ask:

Using my consumption figures, draft a cost-aware operating model as a table: each row a named lever, what it saves, and what it costs in reliability or investigation quality. End with the floor we will not go below. Use only my figures; invent no numbers.

Aim for three levers with a trade-off each, and an explicit reliability floor. Cheapest is not the target. Not graded; useful for the Challenge 6 briefing. Use only official pricing: do not claim that stopping an agent ends all billing.

docs.title: Challenge 5 · Final Incident: Restore Global Check-In Before Peak Departure
docs.text:
Challenge 05 of 06 · Act IV: Major Incident

Time: ~60 min · Run mode: Review plus bounded automation · Access: you decide what is approved and what is automated

Before you start: is your Sev1 plan armed on YOUR alert?

This challenge depends on Challenge 4. Open Incidents → Triggers & response plans and confirm one plan shows Status: On, Severity: Sev1 and Title contains = your alert name ((Get-Content ./scripts/.env.aetherion.json | ConvertFrom-Json).incidentAlertName). Without it your agent never picks the incident up. Other attendees share this subscription: only your own alert may start your agent. If a thread for someone else's alert appears in your agent, tell your proctor.

Situation. Minutes before peak departures, several services fail together under a passenger surge: the flight board is dark, crew scheduling is timing out, check-in has slowed to a crawl, and the API front door is failing partner and mobile traffic.

You are not first on scene. The Sev1 plan you armed matched your alert before anyone paged you, and the agent has been working the incident unattended. Your first job is not to fix something. It is to find out what has already been changed in your absence.

Mission. Take handover from the agent, then restore Aetherion AirOps before peak departure: verify what it changed, triage the rest by business tier, remediate within the runbook guardrails, and verify each service.

Incident timeline Time Event 18:07 A change rolls out to flight-ops 18:12 Check-in / booking latency begins to climb 18:14 Crew scheduling starts timing out under load 18:17 The live flight board goes dark 18:21 The API front door starts failing partner traffic 18:23 Your Sev1 alert fires and auto-triggers your agent 18:25 Major incident declared. You are incident commander

Start this challenge

./scripts/start-challenge.ps1 5

If your Sev1 alert from Challenge 4 is still firing, the script waits (up to about 6 minutes) for it to clear, because a new alert, and so a new agent thread, only appears after the old one resolves. That is normal. Then four faults land at once and the board takes two or three minutes to show all of them. Your alert fires a few minutes later. Do not triage from a half-drawn picture.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Take handover. Find the thread your alert opened by itself, read what the agent changed unattended, and verify it yourself.
  2. Read the whole board. Order the remaining work by business impact (flight board and legal-to-fly first), not the loudest alert.
  3. Check the agent's memory. Ask whether it has seen a similar incident, and let it surface the earlier RCA.
  4. Recover. Fix the remaining tiers with sanctioned, reversible actions. Use the Extra B subagent and skill if you built them; otherwise direct the main agent.
  5. Localize the front door. Compare direct against APIM and treat the policy change as customer-facing.
  6. Verify every service. Confirm each fix from telemetry, then the whole platform green.

docs.title: Suggested prompt
docs.text:
Paste into the [Sev1] <your alert name> thread

You picked this incident up before I did. List every action you took without my approval and how I can verify each one. Then tell me what is still broken and what I should deal with first.

Paste it into the right thread

It only works inside the thread your alert opened. In a fresh chat it answers about whatever it worked on last (validated: it reported on the previous baggage canary while the flight board was 100% down).

docs.title: Success criteria
docs.text:
• You can state exactly what the agent changed without approval, verified from the cluster rather than its summary.
  • Every failing service is triaged by priority and restored with a reversible action, and the API front door serves legitimate traffic again.
  • The platform is healthy, your own Sev1 alert fired and triggered your agent, and check-challenge.ps1 5 passes.

Verify your work

./scripts/check-challenge.ps1 5

It grades the end state and that a Sev1 alert from your environment fired since you started. Fixing everything by hand is not enough.

Hints
  • Triage, don't firefight. Order by business tier. You have solved each of these failure classes before.
  • Service or front door? If the backend is healthy when you hit it directly but clients still fail, the fault is at the API front door.
  • The board may get worse once the front door is fixed: traffic flowing reveals what the outage was masking.
  • Still stuck? Ask: "Read the whole Aetherion board. List every service still failing, order remediation by business tier (flight board and legal-to-fly first), name the sanctioned reversible fix for each, and pull any earlier crew-scheduling or check-in RCA from memory."
Stuck? Step by step Task 1 · Take handover

Treat it like handover from a colleague who has been on the incident ten minutes. Open the thread titled [Sev1] <your alert name> (you did not create it) and paste the prompt above. Then audit the outcome:

kubectl -n aetherion rollout history deployment/flight-ops
kubectl -n aetherion get deploy flight-ops -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}{"\n"}'

Expect it to have acted where the fix is unambiguous and reversible, and held where the call is a judgement. Those held tiers are your work.

If no thread appeared

Check the plan: Status On, Severity Sev1, Title contains = your exact alert name, subagent on Meta Agent, and no other plan. Check Monitor → Alerts shows your alert Fired. If the alert fired and nothing started, tell your proctor: the agent may lack Monitoring Contributor on the subscription. Re-run start-challenge.ps1 5 once fixed.

Task 2 · Read the whole board

List every failing service and order by business tier.

The board cannot see your front door

The Operations Center polls services directly, inside the cluster, so it can read green while every partner and mobile customer gets a 500 at the edge. Always ask the customer-facing question separately. That is Task 5.

Task 3 · Check the agent's memory

Have you investigated a crew-scheduling or check-in slowdown on this platform before? Recall the root cause and which fix worked.

If you saved your Challenge 2 hypothesis (or did Extra A), session insights should surface it. The second incident should cost less than the first.

Task 4 · Recover

Keep actions governed and follow the runbooks: fix the layer that is actually saturated, never delete the database. If you built Extra B, name the subagent and skill explicitly, because neither fires on its own:

Delegate to your aks-triage subagent: which workloads in aetherion are unhealthy, and why? Use the crew-query-path-recovery skill to restore crew scheduling.

The subagent reports and hands back (it has no write tool). Without Extra B, ask the main agent for the same work.

Time the crew tier

Note the minutes to restore crew scheduling and compare with your Challenge 2 number. That gap is the finding you take to Challenge 6, even if it is smaller than you expected.

Task 5 · Localize the front door

Compare backend health directly with the same call through APIM. Direct 200 with APIM failing means the edge policy is at fault.

Run this from your machine, not the agent

The agent's sandbox can block the gateway, returning a proxy 403 before Azure sees the request. Treat "external check failed" as a tooling limit. Confirm from the policy plus your own call:

$st = Get-Content ./scripts/.env.aetherion.json -Raw | ConvertFrom-Json
(Invoke-WebRequest "http://$($st.gatewayIp)/api/status").StatusCode
(Invoke-WebRequest "$($st.apimGatewayUrl)/aetherion/api/status" `
   -Headers @{ 'Ocp-Apim-Subscription-Key' = $st.apimSubscriptionKey }).StatusCode

It can fix the edge because its identity holds API Management Service Contributor, scoped to the APIM service alone: narrow enough to fix this and nothing else.

Task 6 · Verify every service

Confirm each fix from telemetry, not from the agent's summary, then run the check.

Up next: brief leadership

Boarding resumes. Close the incident out for the people who were not on the bridge.

Proceed to Challenge 6 · Leadership Briefing →

docs.title: Challenge 6 · Boarding Resumes: Brief Airline Leadership
docs.text:
Challenge 06 of 06 · Act IV: Major Incident

Time: ~25 min core (+20 min stretch) · Run mode: Review · Access: read-only summarization, plus governed writes to your repo

Situation. The platform is stable and the peak departure bank is away safely. A major incident is not closed when the tiles go green. It is closed when leadership understands it and the team has captured what to do differently.

Mission. Produce a concise leadership briefing, an engineering RCA handover that separates symptom, root cause, mitigation and remaining risk, and a downloadable PDF of the briefing. Stretch: publish the RCA back to your repository.

Start this challenge

./scripts/start-challenge.ps1 6

No fault is injected, so the platform stays green while you write.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Assemble the evidence. Build one defensible narrative from what you preserved during the shift.
  2. Write the leadership briefing. Short, impact-first and non-technical, for the operations director.
  3. Write the engineering RCA handover. Exact actions, how each was verified, open risks and change evidence.
  4. Generate the PDF. Have the agent render the briefing, with a timeline chart, in its Python sandbox.
  5. Stretch · File the RCA as an issue on your repo with the GitHub Connector.
  6. Stretch · Open a pull request that fixes the runbook that failed you, through the GitHub MCP server.

Tasks 5 and 6 need the GitHub token you created during setup. If time is short, finish 1 to 4.

docs.title: Suggested prompt
docs.text:
Paste into the agent chat

From today's preserved evidence, draft two separate artifacts: (1) a concise, impact-first leadership briefing (business impact, root cause, recovery, risk, lessons) and (2) an engineering RCA handover (actions taken, how each was verified, open risks, and change evidence: rollout history with change causes, and the Azure Activity Log for the API Management policy change). Then render the briefing as a PDF with an incident-timeline chart using your Python sandbox.

docs.title: Success criteria
docs.text:
• The platform is healthy at close.
  • The briefing covers impact, root cause, recovery, risk and lessons. The RCA separates symptom, root cause, mitigation and permanent fix, with change evidence from rollout history and the Activity Log.
  • The agent produced a downloadable PDF with a timeline chart.
  • Stretch: the RCA exists as an issue on your repo, and a pull request improves the runbook that failed in Challenge 5.

Verify your work

./scripts/check-challenge.ps1 6

Platform health is graded. The briefing is yours to attest to, and the issue and pull request are checked on your repo if you did the stretch.

Hints
  • Start from the evidence you preserved, not memory. Write two documents: leadership wants impact; the next on-call wants exact actions and open risks.
  • Feed the lessons back into the agent's memory, then get them out of the agent entirely: a record in one agent's memory is still a single point of failure.
Stuck? Step by step Task 2 · Leadership briefing

Write a briefing for the operations director about today's major incident. Lead with business impact. Cover what passengers experienced and for how long, the root cause in plain language, how we recovered, the cost and residual risk, and the lessons. Under one page, no Kubernetes jargon.

If a sentence needs an engineer to translate it, send it back.

Answer \"what did this buy us?\"

Add your two numbers yourself, because the agent cannot know them: minutes to a hypothesis in Challenge 2 (cold) against minutes to recover the crew tier in Challenge 5. State the difference plainly and say it is one day's sample from one team, not a benchmark.

Task 3 · Engineering RCA

Write an engineering RCA handover for the next on-call: every action taken and how it was verified, the remaining risk, and the change-correlation evidence with exact sources.

Workload changes live in rollout history (kubectl rollout history deploy/<svc> -n aetherion). The API Management policy change is in the Azure Activity Log as Set Product policy configuration. In-cluster changes never reach the Activity Log, which is itself a gap worth stating. If the agent finds nothing, ask it to query the Activity Log at subscription scope.

Task 4 · PDF

Render the leadership briefing as a formatted PDF, including an incident timeline chart, using your Python sandbox. Give me a download link.

If the download fails, ask it to list the file and give the link again: the first link can expire.

Task 5 · File the RCA as an issue (stretch)

Code Access (Challenge 1) lets the agent read your repo. Writing needs the GitHub Connector.

  1. Builder → Connectors → Add connector → GitHub. Authenticate with OAuth or a fine-grained PAT with Issues and Pull requests: Read and write. Select your copy of aetherion-airops-platform.

  2. Ask:

    Publish the engineering RCA as a GitHub issue on https://github.com/<your-account>/aetherion-airops-platform. Title it RCA: major incident - global check-in degradation. Include the timeline, root cause per service, every action and how it was verified, and a checklist of corrective actions. Label it incident.

  3. In Review mode you approve the write. Read it first: it goes into a repository with your name on it.

\"No writes\" is a tool boundary, not a permission boundary

Code Access leaves an OAuth credential in the sandbox clone. In Autonomous mode an agent with only Code Access has been seen reading it and filing the issue with gh api. What holds the line is run mode and approvals. Use the connector anyway: it is the governed, auditable path.

Issues work because you made your repo from a template (forks have Issues disabled). Filing an issue records what happened; it does not change what happens next. For that you need a file change, which the connector cannot make because it only opens a PR between branches that already exist. That is Task 6.

Task 6 · Open the pull request (stretch)
  1. Builder → Connectors → Add connector → GitHub (MCP). Transport Streamable-HTTP, URL prefilled, auth with your PAT (no OAuth option here).
  2. The token must allow: Contents, Pull requests, Issues, all Read and write, with Only select repositories set to your private copy. A read-only token connects fine and then fails on the first write, which looks like a broken connector.
  3. A Select tools step lists everything the server exposes. You have 80 tools in total per agent, shared with native tools. Take only what you need, or you will degrade tool selection.
  4. Ask the agent to branch, commit and open a PR that fixes the runbook that failed in Challenge 5.

In an organisation, a fine-grained token may need owner approval before it works.

docs.title: Extra A · Give the Agent Aetherion's Operational Knowledge
docs.text:
Extra A · Optional extra

Time: ~40 min · Run mode: Review, approved writes · Access: every action approved by you

Do this if you finish early. Nothing later depends on it.

Situation. Crew scheduling is failing and Marco Bianchi on the crew desk cannot confirm who is legal to fly the evening wave. Services that share its database are wobbling too, so "the database is down" is the obvious call, and it is wrong. Out of the box the agent gives generic advice, and "restart the database" is exactly what Aetherion's runbooks forbid.

Mission. Ground the agent in Aetherion's runbooks so it recommends the sanctioned fix, then recover crew-scheduling with that non-destructive remediation.

Start this challenge

./scripts/start-challenge.ps1 A

Crew scheduling degrades in two or three minutes and its neighbours follow. Read the whole board before you draw the blast radius.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Find the origin. Work out which service causes the database pressure and which merely share the damage.
  2. Ground the agent. Load the knowledge/ runbooks, then re-ask and watch the advice change.
  3. Apply the sanctioned fix. Repair the query path the runbook points to (never delete the database) and confirm crew recovers.

docs.title: Suggested prompt
docs.text:
Ask this before you load anything, so you have something to compare against.

Paste into the agent chat, ungrounded

crew-scheduling is timing out. The pods aren't CPU-bound and the database is not down. Work out what is saturating the shared database, and tell me what you would do about it.

Keep that answer as your control. Task 2 asks again with the runbooks loaded.

docs.title: Success criteria
docs.text:
• You can name the origin service and explain why its neighbours suffer without being at fault.
  • The grounded agent cites the runbook guardrail (repair the query path, never delete the database) and you apply that fix under approval.
  • /api/crew is back inside the 400 ms budget while the roster rush is still running. A tile that merely answers again is not a pass.

Verify your work

./scripts/check-challenge.ps1 A
Hints
  • More than one service is unhappy, but not equally. Ask what they share, then which of them uses it hardest: that one is the origin. Compare several readings against your baseline, because the neighbours spike rather than sit slow.
  • A busy database is not a broken one. If the pods are comfortable and the database is not, adding pods or connections only sends more work to the part already at its limit.
  • Load the runbooks from your lab clone's knowledge/ folder (the application repo does not carry them).
Stuck? Step by step Task 1 · Find the origin

crew-scheduling is in seconds. Its database-backed neighbours (flight-ops, booking, telemetry-ingest) still serve but spike above your Challenge 1 baseline. baggage, which uses no database, stays flat. That is a shared-dependency problem: one service in trouble, neighbours wobbling.

Ask the agent to put pod CPU next to the PostgreSQL server CPU (kubectl top pods -n aetherion confirms it). Comfortable pods and a saturated database mean the constraint is the work sent to it. Only one service is running a rush against a table it can no longer read efficiently. Give it a few minutes before you judge the neighbours: one early glance shows one red service and three healthy ones, which is the wrong conclusion.

Task 2 · Ground the agent

Builder → Knowledge Sources: add the runbooks from your lab clone's knowledge/ folder.

Add them one at a time, and do not trust the tick

Uploading all seven together can lose the last file, runbook-database.md, which is the one you need, while the page still says Indexed. Add the others first and that one alone at the end. If the agent later answers without citing a runbook, delete it and re-add it alone.

Then ask again in a new chat thread (in the old one it can restate its earlier answer):

crew-scheduling is timing out. The pods aren't CPU-bound and the database is not down. Work out what is saturating the shared database. Use the Aetherion runbooks I loaded, cite the guardrail you follow, and do not delete or restart the database.

Compare with your control. You want what only Aetherion knows: what is forbidden, the escalation path, and why the obvious remedies are wrong. If the answers are identical, the knowledge is not reaching the agent.

Task 3 · Apply the sanctioned fix

Follow the runbook: repair the query path. The autoscaler is not adding replicas (pod CPU is below target), which rules out scaling and a wider connection pool. The fix is a schema change, so keep the agent in Review, tell it to apply, and approve. Then confirm /api/crew is fast, not merely answering.

  • Expect two approvals. The fix runs as a Kubernetes Job, so you approve the Job and, separately, the postgres:16-alpine image it pulls. The second card is not a duplicate.
  • It needs Code Access from Challenge 1. The agent applies the manifest from your copy over HTTPS at a pinned commit. Other routes fail (stdin and its own checked-out copy are rejected).
  • The agent may offer to update the runbook afterwards. Skip keeps the lab stable; Update runbook shows what it would write.

Mission. Build an AKS specialist subagent scoped to the tools it needs (not everything), use it for an investigation, then encode the crew recovery as a skill with its guardrails intact.

Start this challenge

No fault is injected, so the board stays green while you build.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Build the specialist. Create an aks-triage subagent, scope it to its eight tools, verify what it got, then delegate a namespace-health investigation to it.
  2. Encode the skill. Capture the Extra A crew recovery as a reusable skill and confirm it loads.
  3. Decide who owns the skill. The specialist or the main agent, and why.

You do not type either definition from scratch. Both ship in your lab clone (not the application repo):

What File Where it goes The aks-triage subagent agents/aks-triage.agent.yaml The dialog's YAML tab The crew recovery skill skills/crew-query-path-recovery/SKILL.md The SKILL.md editor

Read them before you paste. The point is why these eight tools and not the other 46, and why the guardrails are worded as they are.

docs.title: Suggested prompt
docs.text:
Paste into the agent chat

Delegate this to your aks-triage subagent rather than handling it yourself. Triage pod status, events, rollout history and dependency health for the aetherion namespace, and return a scoped health assessment with likely causes and evidence. Tell me which agent produced the answer.

Ask for the subagent by name

"Act as my AKS specialist" does not invoke it: the main agent just adopts the persona. "Delegate this to your aks-triage subagent" does, and you will see a Parallel subagent execution step in the thread.

docs.title: Success criteria
docs.text:
• The subagent exists and is scoped to a deliberate tool set. You verified through the API that RunKubectlReadCommand is present and RunKubectlWriteCommand is absent.
  • You invoked it by name and its triage is genuinely useful.
  • A skill captures the sanctioned recovery with its guardrails, and loads.
  • You decided who owns the skill (the main agent, not the read-only specialist) and can say why.

Verify your work

./scripts/check-challenge.ps1 B

Nothing here changes the platform, so the check asks you to confirm what you built.

Hints
  • Decide the specialist's remit in one sentence first. A subagent that inherits every tool is a persona in a costume: its "read-only" line is only a request. Tools are enforced; instructions are advisory.
  • Derive the tool list from evidence: what an AKS investigation actually used in Challenges 2 and 3 and Extra A.
  • Encode why not in the skill. "Crew is slow, add replicas" would be actively harmful here.
Stuck? Step by step Task 1 · Build the specialist

Builder → Agent Canvas → + Create subagent. Name it aks-triage. Use the YAML tab, not the Form: four of the eight tools come from the built-in MCP server and do not appear in the Form picker, so a Form-only attempt silently builds a half-scoped specialist. Paste agents/aks-triage.agent.yaml.

Tool Why RunKubectlReadCommand, RunAzCliReadCommands Pods, events, rollout history, configuration system-mcp-monitor_monitor_metrics_query, …_resource_log_query, …_activitylog_list Metrics, container logs, platform changes QueryLogAnalyticsSearch Workspace search when metrics are not enough SearchIncidentKnowledge, SearchMemory Runbooks and earlier incidents

Left out on purpose: RunKubectlWriteCommand (the one that matters: the specialist can no longer change the cluster), RunAzCliWriteCommands, UploadKnowledgeDocument, scheduled-task tools.

Selecting tools replaces the inherited set

It does not add to it, so the list must be complete. Without it the canvas shows Inherits 46 tools · 38 skills: identical to the main agent.

Verify what it got. Do not trust the dialog:

$base = az resource show -g <resource-group> -n <agent-name> --resource-type Microsoft.App/agents `
  --api-version 2026-01-01 --query properties.agentEndpoint -o tsv
$tok = az account get-access-token --resource https://azuresre.ai --query accessToken -o tsv
(Invoke-RestMethod "$base/api/v2/agent/tools" -Headers @{ Authorization = "Bearer $tok" }).data |
  Where-Object enabled | Select-Object category, name | Sort-Object category, name

RunKubectlReadCommand must be present and RunKubectlWriteCommand absent. Then delegate by name and judge it on one question: would this have sped up a real AKS incident?

Task 2 · Encode the skill

Builder → Agent Canvas → + Create skill. Name: crew-query-path-recovery. Two descriptions, two jobs:

  • Description (left panel, behind Edit): when to reach for it. For example: "Use when crew scheduling is slow or timing out and the pods look healthy and underutilised: a saturated shared database, not a saturated workload."
  • description: in the SKILL.md frontmatter: what it does.

Select everything in the editor and replace it with the whole skills/crew-query-path-recovery/SKILL.md (this removes the placeholder). Leave Tools empty, then Create.

Its guardrails are the point: diagnose which layer is saturated; repair the query path with the missing index; never delete or restart the database; do not scale the layer that is merely waiting; propose every write first.

Task 3 · Decide who owns the skill

A subagent is something you delegate to by name. A skill is a procedure the agent draws on. Built together does not mean owned together. Open aks-triage → Skills: left inherited it holds the crew skill. Select only aks_general and diagnostic_cpu so the crew skill falls away (selecting overrides; there is no "off").

Reason Detail Remit Its instructions say do not investigate the database. This is a database query path Capability It has no write tool, and the remedy is to apply an index Ownership The main agent commands the whole board and holds the write tools

A skill belongs to whichever agent has both the remit and the tools to execute it.

A skill does not fire on its own

In validation this skill did not activate during a live investigation of exactly its incident. Asked directly, the agent matched it correctly. Name the skill when you want it used.

docs.title: 2. Get the two repositories
docs.text:
You use two repositories in this NanoHack. Keeping them straight matters: one drives the hack, the other is the "production" application the agent investigates.

What it is You get it by Used for Lab clone This workshop: challenges, scripts, runbooks, the subagent and skill files git clone Running start-challenge / check-challenge, and the knowledge/ files in the optional Extra A Your app repo The Aetherion AirOps application source Use this template The repo you connect the SRE Agent to, and the one it writes to in Challenge 6

a) Clone the lab repo. It drives the hack (challenges + scripts):

git clone https://github.com/abengtss-max/azure-sre-agent-nanohack.git
cd azure-sre-agent-nanohack

b) Create your own copy of the application repo. This is the Aetherion AirOps application source that the Azure SRE Agent connects to for change correlation. It is a template repository, so you get your own standalone copy in one click:

  1. Open https://github.com/abengtss-max/aetherion-airops-platform
  2. Click Use this template → Create a new repository.
  3. Choose your own account as the owner, keep the name aetherion-airops-platform, and create it.

It is created private, which is correct — leave it that way. The agent reads it through the Code Access connection you make in Challenge 1, not anonymously.

You'll connect the SRE Agent to your copy in Challenge 1.

Why a template and not a fork

A fork would work, but GitHub turns Issues off on every new fork and Challenge 6 has the agent file the incident RCA as an issue. A template copy arrives with Issues already enabled, so that failure never happens.

Creating it under your personal account also avoids the token-approval step in c) below.

The copy starts with a single commit rather than the upstream history. Nothing in the hack depends on that history: Challenge 3 correlates change from the Kubernetes rollout history, and reads the repo only to answer "what does the manifest declare".

c) Create a GitHub Personal Access Token now. Challenge 6 has the agent write back to your repo — it files the incident RCA as an issue and opens a pull request — and the GitHub MCP connector it uses for that accepts a PAT only. There is no OAuth option on that connector.

Go straight to github.com/settings/personal-access-tokens/new (Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens → Fine-grained tokens) and fill it in like this:

Field Set it to Token name aetherion-microhack Expiration Custom → tomorrow's date. The token only has to outlive today Resource owner your own account Repository access Only select repositories → aetherion-airops-platform Repository permissions → Contents Read and write — create a branch and commit Repository permissions → Pull requests Read and write — open the PR Repository permissions → Issues Read and write — file the RCA

Click Generate token and copy it now — GitHub shows it once. Keep it in your password manager until Challenge 6.

Prefer a classic token? github.com/settings/tokens/new with the top-level repo scope works too.

docs.title: You are the new reliability team for a global airline platform
docs.text:
Aetherion AirOps is a fictional, Tier 0 airline operations platform running on Microsoft Azure. It is the digital backbone of a global carrier's day-to-day flying: it runs flight operations and dispatch, crew scheduling, passenger booking and check-in, baggage tracking, aircraft telemetry ingestion, and the airport and operational dashboards that controllers watch during every shift.

The platform is Tier 0 because when it degrades, aircraft do not move on time. A slow check-in service strands passengers at the gate. A crew-scheduling outage stops duty managers from confirming who is legal to fly. A dark flight board removes the operational picture an entire operations center depends on. The impact is measured in delayed departures, missed connections, stranded baggage, service-level breaches, and reputational damage.

Today you join Aetherion AirOps as its new Site Reliability Engineering team. You will run a shift inside the Global Operations Center, take a series of real incidents as they unfold, and use Azure SRE Agent to investigate, recommend and recover — with you deciding what it is allowed to do, and when. The guardrails are the same ones a real airline would insist on.

This is an operational and business platform built for learning. It is not safety-of-flight avionics and it does not control real aircraft. Every fault in this NanoHack is deliberately injected and fictional.

docs.title: Who you'll be working with
docs.text:
You share the Operations Center with four others. You meet them as the day brings them in — you don't need to remember them now.

  • Sam Rivera · Reliability engineer

    This is you. Your first week in Aetherion's Global Operations Center, walking into a shift that will not stay quiet. Every operational decision today is yours to make.

  • Aria · Azure SRE Agent

    Your AI teammate for the shift. The hologram beside you in every scene is the Azure SRE Agent. Treat it like a new SRE joining the team: in Challenge 1 you onboard it, scope what it can see, and decide what it is allowed to do.

  • Elena Vasquez · Operations director

    Answers for the airline. Wants incidents resolved safely, with a human in the loop, and expects them explained in business terms afterwards.

  • Marco Bianchi · Crew duty manager

    Runs the crew desk. When crew scheduling degrades, Marco cannot verify which crew are rested, qualified and legal to fly — and aircraft do not depart without that answer.

  • Priya Nair · FinOps analyst

    Watches what the platform and the agent cost. Autonomy only counts as a win if it improves outcomes without turning into runaway spend.

That spread is deliberate. Whether an agent earns a place in production is never just an operator's call — it is decided by execution, governance, business continuity and cost together. You will hear from all four today.

docs.title: The shift ahead: challenge map
docs.text:
Read down the list and you are also reading the agent's arc: it starts read-only and supervised, then recovers under your approval, and only then is trusted to act on its own — still inside limits you set.

# Challenge What you practice 1 Onboard the Agent and Establish the Baseline Connect the agent read-only, capture a baseline + a daily proactive health check 2 Detect and Investigate Without Touching Production Detect a symptom, then read-only telemetry/log correlation and a defensible hypothesis 3 Controlled Recovery Human-approved remediation of the check-in incident 4 Autonomous Recovery and Sev1 Plan Let the agent fix a bounded incident on its own, then arm the Sev1 response plan 5 Final Incident: Restore Global Check-In Before Peak Departure End-to-end multi-fault response as incident commander 6 Boarding Resumes: Brief Airline Leadership Incident summary and leadership handover

Optional extras if you finish early: Extra A (give the agent Aetherion's operational knowledge) and Extra B (a specialist subagent and a reusable skill).

docs.title: How the day works
docs.text:
The challenges form one continuous storyline, not a set of unrelated tutorials. Each challenge begins where the last one ended: the baseline you capture early is the evidence you compare against later; the permissions you reason about become the approvals you rely on; the autonomy you earn and the Sev1 plan you arm are what meet you in the final incident.

Challenges unlock linearly: you finish one before the next opens. You drive each challenge yourself with two commands:

./scripts/start-challenge.ps1 <N>   # opens the incident for challenge N (root cause hidden)
./scripts/check-challenge.ps1 <N>   # validates the required end state and unlocks challenge N+1
  • start-challenge.ps1 injects the incident (or sets up a configuration exercise) without telling you the root cause. That is your job to find.
  • check-challenge.ps1 verifies the real end state against the live cluster and API Management, then unlocks the next challenge. A symptom-only or "wait it out" fix will not pass. The underlying fault must genuinely be cleared.

Work from evidence. Each challenge gives you the scenario, the business stakes, the signals you can inspect, the guardrails, and progressive hints, which is enough to investigate and solve it yourself. Start read-only, use the least privilege that gets the job done, and let write actions go through approval unless a challenge explicitly enables bounded automation. Verify recovery with telemetry after every change, and preserve the evidence you will need for the incident summary at the end of the shift.

Use the agent to do the work; use kubectl to check the agent. You have a terminal, and some of these incidents would be faster to fix by hand. Resist it. The point of the day is to find out where an agent earns its place and where it doesn't, and you learn nothing about that by racing it. Where a challenge does ask you to run something directly, it is to verify a claim the agent made — auditing an agent through the agent tells you nothing.

Challenges 2 and 3 are one ongoing incident: detection and read-only investigation, then controlled recovery.

Your shift starts now

The board is green, Aria is waiting, and nothing is on fire yet. Go and find out what healthy looks like before something isn't.

Start Challenge 1 →

docs.title: Azure portal walkthrough
docs.text:
New to Azure or to the SRE Agent? This page is your complete, click-by-click reference for every action the challenges ask you to perform. Each challenge links back to the exact procedures below, so you never have to guess where a button is.

Portal UI may vary

Azure portal labels and blades occasionally move. When a screen differs from a step here, follow the matching step in the linked official doc. The flow is the same. Keep the Azure portal open in one tab and this page in another.

Everything in this hack uses the same defaults:

Setting Value Resource group rg-aetherion-microhack-<suffix> (your unique name) Region swedencentral AKS cluster aetherion-aks (namespace aetherion) SRE Agent aetherion-sre-agent

Your resource group name is unique

Provisioning always creates rg-aetherion-microhack-<suffix> (for example rg-aetherion-microhack-a7c3) and prints the exact name at the end. Wherever this guide says the resource group, use your suffixed name.

docs.title: A · Sign in to the Azure portal
docs.text:
1. Open https://portal.azure.com and sign in with the account that owns the subscription you provisioned.
  2. Confirm the correct directory/subscription: select your avatar (top-right) → Switch directory if you have more than one.
  3. In the top search bar, type your resource group name (rg-aetherion-microhack-<suffix>) and open it. Pin it (the star icon) so it's one click away all day.

docs.title: B · Open the Operations Center
docs.text:
The Operations Center is the live health board you use to detect and verify every incident.

  1. The provisioning script opened it automatically. If you lost the tab, get the URL again by running in your terminal: 
    $st = Get-Content ./scripts/.env.aetherion.json | ConvertFrom-Json
if ($st.httpsUrl) { $st.httpsUrl } else { "http://$($st.gatewayIp)/" }
  2. Open that URL (HTTPS if configured). Let the page settle. The flight board, service tiles and operational-risk gauge should all render.
  3. Healthy reference: every service tile is green and the risk gauge is low. This is what you compare against when something breaks.

docs.title: C · Open Grafana and sign in
docs.text:
1. In the portal search bar, type Grafana and open Azure Managed Grafana → the aetherion workspace → Endpoint URL.
  2. Sign in with your Azure account (single sign-on). If prompted for access, you need at least Grafana Viewer on the workspace.
  3. Open the Aetherion dashboard. Confirm data is flowing in two panels: AKS (pods / CPU) and Application Insights (requests / latency).

docs.title: D · Create the SRE Agent
docs.text:
Do this once, in Challenge 1. Creating the agent and setting it up are two separate steps. Create alone grants no access to your app.

  1. In the portal search bar, type Azure SRE Agent and select it.
  2. Select Create.
  3. On Basics, set:
    • Subscription: your subscription.
    • Resource group: your provisioned group (rg-aetherion-microhack-<suffix>).
    • Name: aetherion-sre-agent.
    • Region: the closest supported region (e.g. swedencentral).
    • Application Insights: choose Create new. The agent provisions its own App Insights + Log Analytics for its own telemetry. This is separate from the app's aetherion-law / aetherion-appi.
    • Model provider: Azure OpenAI is a good default (lower cost, stays in the EU data boundary).
  4. Leave the default managed identity option so the agent gets its own identity.
  5. Select Review + create → Create and wait for deployment to finish.
  6. Open the resource and confirm the chat/console loads.

Reference: Create and set up · Complete your setup

docs.title: D2 · Set up your agent: connect context
docs.text:
In the agent, run Set up your agent (Full setup) and connect three sources:

  1. Code → GitHub → sign in → add your copy of aetherion-airops-platform (used for change correlation in Challenge 3).
  2. Logs → Log Analytics Workspace → pick the app's aetherion-law (not the agent's own auto-created workspace).
  3. Azure resources → set the scope to Resource group, select only your app resource group, and pick the Reader permission level.

Scope the agent to the app resource group only

Do not choose Subscription or Management group scope. Resource-group scope keeps the agent focused on just this application.

Knowledge is connected later, in Extra A, not here.

docs.title: E · Give the agent read-only (Reader) access
docs.text:
The Set up your agent wizard (section D2) already grants this. Do it manually here only if you skipped the wizard's Azure resources step. Reader lets the agent see the resource group; in Review mode it still asks before any change.

  1. Open your resource group (rg-aetherion-microhack-<suffix>) → Access control (IAM).
  2. Select Add → Add role assignment.
  3. Role: search and pick Reader.
  4. Members: choose Managed identity → select the aetherion-sre-agent identity.
  5. Select Review + assign.
  6. Back in the agent, ask it to "list the resources in the resource group and summarise the application" to confirm scope.

Permissions vs. run mode

Creating and setting up the agent grants its identity Monitoring Contributor plus a reader bundle, so the identity is not strictly read-only. The guarantee that it won't change anything without you comes from the Review run mode (section F), not from the role.

Reference: Manage roles and permissions

docs.title: F · Set the run mode (Review vs Autonomous)
docs.text:
1. Open the aetherion-sre-agent resource → Settings (or the run-mode control in the agent console).
  2. Review (default): the agent proposes a plan and waits for your approval before any write. Use this for Acts I-III.
  3. Autonomous: the agent executes approved classes of action without pausing. Only switch a specific, validated fault to Autonomous (Challenge 4).
  4. Changing run mode is approved by the SRE Agent Administrator role.

docs.title: G · Ask the agent / start a thread
docs.text:
1. Open the agent resource → the chat/console.
  2. Type a specific question, for example "Give an operational baseline for the aetherion namespace: services, ready replicas, dependencies, and check-in latency."
  3. When the agent proposes a write in Review mode, it shows a plan with an Approve / Reject prompt. Read the plan, because that plan is your approval artifact, then decide.

docs.title: H · Approve a write, or grant a narrow write role
docs.text:
When a fix needs a change, you have two governed paths.

Approve it in Review modeGrant a scoped role
  1. Ask the agent for a remediation plan, and read it.
  2. A plan on its own queues nothing. Tell the agent to apply it — the approval card appears when it attempts the write, not when it finishes thinking.
  3. Read the exact command on the card, then select Approve action.

The card states "Agent permissions will be used to complete this action." The write runs as the agent's own managed identity, so the change is attributed in the Activity Log to the agent rather than to you. Your approval is recorded in the thread, not on the resource.

Best when you want a human decision on each change.

  1. Decide the narrowest role that covers the action (e.g. a write role on the AKS cluster only, not the whole subscription).
  2. Open the target resource → Access control (IAM) → Add role assignment → pick the role → Managed identity → aetherion-sre-agent → Review + assign.
  3. Best when the agent needs to reach something it currently cannot, rather than when you want a decision point.

On-behalf-of (OBO)

The docs describe an OBO path where an action runs using your credentials. It is not available in this environment — attempts return "OBO flow is not supported with CliInAdc enabled". Everything the agent does here runs as its own identity, which is why scoping that identity matters.

Reference: Security overview

docs.title: I · Load the knowledge base (ground the agent)
docs.text:
1. In the agent, open Builder → Knowledge Sources.
  2. Upload the Markdown files from your lab clone's knowledge/ folder. The application repo does not contain them.
  3. Check every file reaches Indexed. Bulk upload can partially fail.
  4. Re-ask your remediation question. The advice should now cite Aetherion's own runbook guardrails instead of generic steps.

Reference: Team onboarding & memory

docs.title: J · Create a specialist subagent
docs.text:
1. In the agent, open Builder → Agent Canvas, then click + Create subagent.
  2. Custom agent name: aks-triage.
  3. Instructions: a narrow remit, "AKS reliability triage for the aetherion namespace: pod status, events, rollout history, dependency health." Say how it should behave and what it should do when the evidence points outside its scope, not just what it covers.
  4. Scope the Tools panel deliberately. Left alone the subagent inherits all 46 tools, which makes it a persona rather than a specialist. Selecting tools replaces the inherited set instead of adding to it, so your list has to be complete, not a highlight reel. Extra B gives the exact eight tools and the reason for each. Instructions are advisory; the tool list is what is actually enforced.
  5. Leave Skills inherited while you build. Who owns which skill is a deliberate decision you make in Extra B, Task 3.
  6. Create, then use it by asking the main agent to delegate to it by name ("delegate this to your aks-triage subagent"). Asking the agent to "act as" a specialist does not invoke the subagent. It just adopts the persona.

The Form / YAML toggle edits the same definition and exposes handoff_description, agent_type and enable_skills.

Reference: Subagents & extensibility

docs.title: K · Create a reusable skill
docs.text:
1. Same place: Builder → Agent Canvas → + Create skill (or Builder → Skill Builder).
  2. Name it, then click Edit on Description and describe when the skill should be reached for. The description is what the agent matches the situation against, so a vague one means the skill is never considered. Do not assume a skill fires on its own. Name it when you want it used.
  3. In the pre-scaffolded SKILL.md, fill in the name / description frontmatter and encode a well-defined procedure (e.g. the crew query-path recovery) as steps, keeping the guardrails (confirm which layer is saturated, repair the query path, never delete the database).
  4. Create.

Reference: Skills

docs.title: L · Review agent consumption (AAUs)
docs.text:
1. In the agent, open Settings → Agent Consumption.
  2. Break usage down by thread type (Chats, Incidents, Scheduled tasks, Triggers) and by thread, to see where Azure Agent Units (AAUs) go.
  3. Use only real figures from your environment or the official pricing & billing doc. Never invent rates or savings.

docs.title: M · Inspect AKS (pods, events, rollout)
docs.text:
You can let the agent do this, or check directly:

  • In the portal: resource group → aetherion-aks → Workloads → select a deployment (e.g. flight-ops) → Pods and Events.
  • In your terminal (read-only): 
    kubectl get pods -n aetherion
kubectl describe deploy flight-ops -n aetherion
kubectl rollout history deploy/flight-ops -n aetherion

docs.title: N · Correlate a change with rollout history & the Activity Log
docs.text:
1. For workload changes, start with the cluster's own change record: 
    kubectl rollout history deploy/<service> -n aetherion
    Each revision carries the change cause recorded with it.
  2. For Azure-resource changes (for example an API Management policy), open the resource or resource group → Activity log and filter by the time the tile went red.
  3. Note the gap: changes applied straight to the cluster never appear in the Activity Log, which is exactly why teams route changes through a pipeline. Proximity in time is your strongest lead for a change-induced outage.

docs.title: O · Compare direct-vs-APIM (front-door problems)
docs.text:
When clients fail but the backend looks healthy, the problem is at the front door:

# Load env once
$st = Get-Content ./scripts/.env.aetherion.json | ConvertFrom-Json

# Through the API front door (APIM)
Invoke-WebRequest "$($st.apimGatewayUrl)/aetherion/api/status" `
  -Headers @{ 'Ocp-Apim-Subscription-Key' = $st.apimSubscriptionKey } -UseBasicParsing

# Direct to the service (bypasses APIM). If this is 200, the service is fine
Invoke-WebRequest "http://$($st.gatewayIp)/api/status" -UseBasicParsing

If direct returns 200 but APIM fails, the fault is an API Management policy, not the service.

Return to any challenge. Each one tells you exactly which of these procedures to run, in order.

docs.title: What is the Azure SRE Agent?
docs.text: Azure SRE Agent is an AI teammate for operating production on Azure. It watches your live estate, investigates incidents like an experienced site reliability engineer, explains the likely root cause with evidence, and, with your approval or within guardrails you set, remediates. It reasons across every tier: containers (AKS), the API front door (APIM), databases, caches, and the telemetry that ties them together, not just one service.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• Detects & triages: correlates metrics, logs, traces, resource health and recent changes (Azure Activity Log + GitHub) to find what broke and when.
  • Investigates read-only: produces an evidence-backed root-cause hypothesis before anyone touches production.
  • Remediates safely: proposes a least-disruptive plan you approve, or acts autonomously within a bounded, RBAC-scoped posture.
  • Learns your operations: grounds in your runbooks and architecture, and remembers past incidents so recurrences resolve faster.
  • Extends to your team: custom specialist subagents, reusable skills, alert-triggered response plans, scheduled health checks, and a Python sandbox for reports.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
• Faster recovery (lower MTTR): tireless, parallel investigation shrinks the time from alert to root cause.
  • Less on-call toil: routine triage and well-understood fixes are handled for you, so engineers focus on the hard problems.
  • Governed by design: every action runs under Azure RBAC and is attributable and auditable; you decide how much autonomy to grant.
  • Consistent & institutional: the same sanctioned runbook steps run every time, and hard-won knowledge doesn't leave with the on-call.

You'll build exactly this across the hack

Onboard it read-only, investigate an incident, recover under approval, ground it in your runbooks, engineer a subagent + skill, let it recover autonomously within guardrails, command a major incident, and brief leadership.

docs.title: How you control it: two independent dials
docs.text:
Permissions (Azure RBAC, what the agent's identity is allowed to do) and run mode (how it acts: Review proposes and waits for approval; Autonomous acts within its permissions and guardrails) are the two controls that matter all day. You start read-only and earn autonomy.

Control Options What it decides Permissions (Azure RBAC) Reader → narrow scoped write What the agent's identity is allowed to do Run mode Review · Autonomous How it acts: propose-and-wait vs act within guardrails

Everything else, including skills vs subagents, the knowledge base, and the agent's own telemetry resources, is in The rest of the picture below. Read it once when you have a spare minute; you do not need it all before you start.

Documentation you will return to all day: Overview · Permissions & run modes

docs.title: The rest of the picture
docs.text:
Read this once when convenient. The two dials above are the core; everything here rounds out the picture.

  • Approved writes run as the agent's identity, not yours, so the Activity Log attributes them to the agent.
  • On-behalf-of (OBO), where an action runs under your credentials, is not available in this environment. That is precisely why scoping the agent's own identity matters.
  • Subagents are invoked explicitly, in natural language, by naming the one you want ("delegate this to your aks-triage subagent"). There is no slash-command syntax, and asking the agent to act as a specialist does not invoke one, it just adopts the persona.
  • Skills are matched against their description rather than guaranteed to fire. Name the skill when you want it used. Skills are capped at 5 concurrent active at a time.
  • Only a user with the Azure SRE Agent Administrator role can approve proposed actions.
  • The knowledge base accepts Markdown/text files (this repo's knowledge/), which is how you ground the agent in Aetherion's runbooks and standards.
  • Creating an agent also provisions its own Application Insights, Log Analytics, and managed identity, separate from the application's telemetry.

Documentation you will return to all day: Overview · Create and set up · Complete your setup · Permissions & run modes · Security overview · Team onboarding & memory · Subagents & extensibility · Skills · Agent hooks · Pricing & billing

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Aetherion AirOps is a microservices estate on Azure Kubernetes Service, fronted by Azure API Management, backed by PostgreSQL and Redis, and observed through Application Insights, Log Analytics, managed Prometheus and Grafana. The Azure SRE Agent reasons across every tier, not just the cluster.

docs.title: Environment at a glance
docs.text: Request/data flow runs left to right (solid blue); telemetry and control flow to observability and the Azure SRE Agent (dashed purple); alerting is shown in red. Click the diagram to open it full size. The agent runs governed remediation back into APIM and AKS, correlating change via Azure Activity Log and GitHub history.

docs.title: Executive view
docs.text: The business-level picture: traffic enters through the API front door, flows to the Aetherion AirOps services and their data, and the Azure SRE Agent watches and recovers across every tier, grounded in monitoring, source control and your runbooks. Click to open full size.

docs.title: Where faults hide
docs.text:
The symptom almost always appears at the edge (APIM 5xx or timeouts), but the root cause can live in any tier. The hack deliberately rotates incidents across the gateway, the cluster and the database so attendees learn to reason across the whole estate.

Tier Example fault First signal Edge (APIM) A backend override published to the product policy Gateway 5xx while services are healthy Compute (AKS) A release pinned to an image that can't be pulled Pods never start, the tile goes dark Compute (AKS) A resource limit cut too far CPU throttling, latency climbs under load App rollout A canary revision serving the wrong API surface A slice of requests fails, the rest succeed Data (PostgreSQL) A query with no supporting index over a grown table Database CPU saturated, pods idle and waiting

docs.title: Observability plane
docs.text:
• Operations Center GUI: live service health, operational-risk gauge, flight map, incidents and business impact. First place to confirm a symptom.
  • Application Insights (aetherion-appi): requests, dependencies, exceptions and the application map.
  • Log Analytics (aetherion-law): container and node logs for deep-dive KQL.
  • Managed Prometheus (Azure Monitor workspace aetherion-amw-*): pod and node CPU/memory time series scraped from AKS. This is what makes "is it CPU-bound or is it waiting?" answerable rather than a guess.
  • Azure Managed Grafana: metrics, traces and autoscaling correlation.
  • Azure Activity Log + GitHub: change history for incident correlation.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text: All scripts live in scripts/ and are PowerShell 7 (pwsh). Run them from the repository root, signed in with az login and the correct subscription selected. .sh equivalents exist for the cross-platform ones.
